data.headline: Special Weather Statement issued November 2 at 3:17PM EST by NWS Miami FL
data.description:
At 317 PM EST, National Weather Service meteorologists were tracking
a strong thunderstorm capable of producing a funnel cloud near
Homestead General Airport, moving north at 10 mph.

HAZARD...Funnel clouds and wind gusts of 50 to 55 mph.

SOURCE...Radar indicated.

IMPACT...Funnel clouds occasionally touch down and produce tornadoes
or waterspouts. Gusty winds could knock down tree limbs and
blow around unsecured objects.

Locations impacted include...
Homestead, Homestead Miami Speedway, Homestead General Airport, The
Redland, Florida City, Naranja, Royal Palm Ranger, Leisure City,
Shark Valley Obs Tower, Fortymile Bend, Homestead Base, Princeton,
Everglades National Park, and Inlikita.
data.instruction:
These winds can down small tree limbs and branches, and blow around
unsecured small objects. Seek shelter in a safe building until the
storm passes.

Funnel clouds occasionally touch down and produce tornadoes or
waterspouts. Move indoors and stay away from windows.

data.headline: Coastal Flood Advisory issued November 2 at 1:41AM EST until November 3 at 7:00PM EST by NWS Miami FL
data.description:
* WHAT...Minor to Moderate coastal flooding and dangerous rip
currents.

* WHERE...Coastal Miami Dade County.

* WHEN...Through Tuesday.

* IMPACTS...Flooding of lots, parks, and roads with only
isolated road closures expected. Rip currents can sweep even
the best swimmers away from shore into deeper water.
data.instruction:
If travel is required, allow extra time as some roads may be
closed. Do not drive around barricades or through water of
unknown depth. Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone
property.

Swim near a lifeguard. If caught in a rip current, relax and
float. Don't swim against the current. If able, swim in a
direction following the shoreline. If unable to escape, face the
shore and call or wave for help.

data.headline: Flood Watch issued November 1 at 11:59PM EST until November 2 at 7:00PM EST by NWS Miami FL
data.description:
An upper level low will will continue to influence storms in the
Gulf and Bahamas through Monday. With the lack of a strong synoptic
surface forcing mechanism, predictability as to where and when heavy
rain will fall remains low. However, the environment continues to
support the potential for heavy rainfall and slow moving cells.

* WHAT...Heavy rain may cause, or worsen ongoing urban and street
flooding.

* WHERE...All of South Florida

* WHEN...Through Monday evening.

* IMPACTS...Isolated to scattered areas of flash flooding will be
possible, with the main impact being street flooding, road
closures, and limited impact to structures in flood prone areas.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- Pockets of very heavy rainfall resulted in localized flash
flooding on Sunday and those areas, and others, have the
potential to be impacted again on Monday. Forecast amounts look
very similar to yesterday, with common amounts of 1 to 3 inches
where showers and storms occur. Scattered locations around south
Florida may see closer to 3 to 5 inches of rain. The more
isolated high end amounts have the potential to peak around 6 to
9 inches. These amounts could accumulate rather quickly, on the
order of 2 to 4 hours.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
data.instruction:
You should monitor later forecasts and be alert for possible Flood
Warnings. Those living in areas prone to flooding should be prepared
to take action should flooding develop.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Miami FL
1259 PM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

...New AVIATION...

.KEY MESSAGES...
Updated at 1257 PM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

  - Flood watch remains in effect for all of South Florida as the 
    potential for additional heavy rainfall and flooding 
    continues.

  - Minor to Moderate coastal flooding expected during times of 
    high tide.

  - Dangerous marine and beach conditions are expected across the
    Atlantic coast.

&&

.MESOSCALE UPDATE FOR HEAVY RAINFALL... 
Issued at 1202 PM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

The aforementioned shortwave across the eastern Gulf continues to
enhance upper level divergence across South Florida early this 
afternoon, enhancing low level convergence and facilitating a 
gradual spatial expansion of shower and thunderstorm activity 
across the region. 17z Mesoanalysis in tandem with GOES east 
imagery indicates a corridor of enhanced surface heating across 
the southeastern half of the Florida Peninsula, resulting in the 
development of a differential heating boundary across the 
peninsula with the influence of sprawling cold pools, 1) across 
southwestern Florida and the 2) second more pronounced cold pool 
just north of Lake Okeechobee and across the majority of the 
Treasure Coast. Across southeastern Florida, diurnal heating has 
resulted in temperatures in the low to mid 80s with a lull in 
activity across the majority of metro Miami-Dade and Broward 
counties. SBCAPE and MUCAPE analysis indicates enough instability 
remains in the low level boundary layer for additional convection
along and to the south of mesoscale boundaries with a foci in 
near-term activity across Palm Beach County and the Lake 
Okeechobee region. While 500mb flow is out of a more southerly 
component today, as opposed to the inverse 1km (easterly)/6km 
(westerly) orientation that led to efficient coastal convergence 
(and a high- end maxima of 15+" of rainfall across Palm Beach 
County) yesterday, slow movement of showers and thunderstorms and
upstream growth (backbuilding) could re- aggravate urban flooding
across areas that remain completely saturated/inundated from a 
soil moisture perspective. A Flood Watch remains in effect for all
of South Florida through 7PM this evening with a close eye being 
kept on the latest trends with radar coverage and rainfall totals 
as the afternoon progresses for any need of watch extension.

Recent ACARS soundings from FLL/MIA depict some residual CIN and 
drier air in the vertical column that may act to suppress more
robust convection across metro Miami-Dade and Broward in the near
term. This residual inhibition and drier air in the column may be
largely responsible for the break in activity that has been 
observed for much of today across most east coast locales. 
Although that trend has recently come to a close across northern 
and central Palm Beach County where convection continues to back- 
build along locales that certainly don't need any additional 
precipitation. Given the forcing aloft and the pocket of residual 
instability across these areas that have received ample surface 
heating, additional showers and thunderstorms could still 
materialize across the eastern half of South Florida for the 
remainder of today. The 12z HREF LPMM has a widespread 1-2" across
most of the northeastern half of South Florida through 7am on 
Wednesday. The threat of isolated higher rainfall amounts greater 
than 3-5" inches remains possible along the east coast metro and 
the Weather Prediction Center maintained a Slight Risk (level 2 of
4) of excessive rainfall for the entire east coast of South 
Florida for the remainder of today. Short fused Flood Advisories 
and Flash Flood Warnings may be needed if heavy rainfall falls 
over areas that received several inches of rainfall within the 
past 24 hours.

&&

.SYNOPSIS...
Issued at 327 AM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

Water vapor imagery and model analysis fields show an elongated
shortwave extending from the southeast Gulf, through the Southeast
and into the Mid-Atlantic where it connects in with the northern
stream flow. There's very little surface reflection to this upper
low, with the latest WPC surface analysis depicting high pressure
centered over the Mid-Atlantic/NW Atlantic, with its western
reaches covering much of the eastern CONUS. Locally, we remain
under easterly flow at the base of the ridge with a coastal trough
still established down the east coast of Florida. Additionally, an
MCV is likely still present across Central Florida as a result of
yesterday's storms.

&&

.SHORT TERM...
(Today through Tuesday)
Issued at 327 AM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

We enter another very low predictability period today with the
environment primed to produce more heavy rainfall should a surface
focus emerge. CAMs have struggled to identify the ongoing precip
pattern and thus low confidence exists regarding their future
predictions. Some of the CAMs that at least more closely resemble
the ongoing pattern would suggest banding features along the east
coast where upslope flow coincides with mesoscale boundaries
through mid-afternoon. They also depict convection in the SE Gulf,
associated with the upper low, moving across south Florida through
the afternoon and evening. As the storms from the Gulf reach the
east coast, a period of slow moving storms producing heavy
rainfall will be possible. Forecast rain amounts look very 
similar to yesterday, with common amounts of 1 to 3 inches where 
showers and storms occur. Scattered locations around south Florida
may see closer to 3 to 5 inches of rain. The more isolated high 
end amounts have the potential to peak around 6 to 9 inches. These
amounts could accumulate rather quickly, on the order of 2 to 4 
hours. The Flood Watch will continue through today and has been
expanded over all of South Florida due to low confidence in where
the heaviest rain will setup.

As the base of the elongated trough cuts off over the SE Gulf
today, it will be slow to move out of the region and likely have
to wait for an approaching northern stream frontal system to nudge
it through south Florida. This will likely mean a continued wet
pattern through Tuesday. However, the good news is that dry mid-
level air, associated with the part of the shortwave that will
advect into the Atlantic, may result in lower PWATs and less
forcing. This means an overall lower top-end to expected rain
amounts. Expect common rainfall amounts on Tuesday closer to 1-2"
with localized higher amounts in the 2-4" range. Not nothing, but
better than Sunday and Today. It also look as though most of the
rainfall on Tuesday will be confined to the east coast.

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Tuesday night through Sunday)
Issued at 327 AM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

With the aforementioned mid-week frontal system, models are
struggling with whether the shortwave cuts off and loses latitude
from the northern stream. In solutions where it cuts off the
shortwave it has a much slower progression across the CONUS. This
will ultimately influence when/if we get frontal passage across
south Florida late this week. Regardless, models tend to keep the
frontal passage pretty dry, this far south, and also have very
little signal for any anomalous sensible weather fields in the
extended range. 

The slow nudge of the frontal system will displace the ridge axis
further north. This will remove the direct easterly component and
calm winds a bit. Both of these results mean that we'll probably
have less precipitation across south Florida from mid-week onward.

&&

.AVIATION...
(18Z TAFS)
Issued at 1257 PM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

Increasing SHRA/TSRA may result in bouts of sub MVFR cigs/vis at
terminals this afternoon/evening. Gusty erratic winds may occur
with any SHRA/TSRA that directly impacts a terminal. Winds are
forecast to lessen after sunset with a continuation of SHRA/TSRA
across the region through the end of the TAF period. 

&&

.MARINE...
Issued at 327 AM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

Hazardous marine conditions will continue across the Atlantic waters 
through the early portion of the week as a fresh to strong easterly 
breeze remains in place combined with a lingering northeasterly 
swell. Across the Gulf waters, a moderate to fresh easterly breeze 
will continue today before gradually starting to diminish on 
Tuesday. Scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms will 
continue across all local waters through the early portion of the 
week. 

&&

.BEACHES...
Issued at 327 AM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

The onshore flow and elevated winds and seas will keep a High Risk
for rip currents across Atlantic beaches well into this week.
Large breakers are expected through at least this morning across
Broward and Palm beaches, with a high surf advisory in effect 
for these locations. Higher than usual tides will also create 
elevated water levels near the coast. Dangerous beach and swim 
conditions are expected through mid-week.

&&

.HYDROLOGY...
Issued at 327 AM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

Water levels are forecast to gradually start climbing into
Moderate flood stage again by tonight's high tide as we start to 
head closer and closer to the New Moon on Nov 9. Hopefully, by 
mid-week, we'll be able to remove the strong onshore wind 
component and pull back some of the heavy rain potential as 
astronomical tide levels start to rise again.

&&

TWOAT 

Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
100 PM EST Mon Nov 2 2026

For the North Atlantic...Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of America:

Western Atlantic:
An area of low pressure is likely to form along a weakening frontal 
boundary a few hundred miles northeast of the Bahamas in a couple of 
days. This system could acquire some subtropical characteristics 
late this week while it drifts over the western Atlantic. The 
chances of subtropical development should end by the weekend when 
the system is expected to move eastward or northeastward into 
unfavorable environmental conditions.
* Formation chance through 48 hours...low...near 0 percent.
* Formation chance through 7 days...low...30 percent.

$$
Forecaster Cangialosi
